theme: Graphite GPU, Skia m152, and memory fixes
highlights_headline: SkiaSharp 4.152.0 updates the engine to Skia m152 and ships Graphite GPU backend bindings for Vulkan, Metal, and Dawn.
highlights_body: The new Graphite rendering pipeline is now available for all three GPU backends. Several native memory safety fixes land alongside further performance improvements and Nano Server FreeType font support.

bullets.detail: The engine is now built from Skia chrome/m152, bringing the latest upstream rendering improvements and GPU fixes.
An additional upstream sync from the chrome/m151 branch applies engine stability improvements before the m152 update.

bullets.lead: Graphite GPU backend bindings for Vulkan, Metal, and Dawn
bullets.detail: New bindings expose Skia's next-generation Graphite rendering pipeline. Consumers can now create Graphite GPU contexts for Vulkan, Metal, and Dawn backends, unlocking the modern lower-overhead GPU path.

bullets.lead: Backend-neutral async RequestReadPixels on SKImage and SKSurface
bullets.detail: A new async ReadPixels API lets callers read pixel data from GPU-backed images and surfaces without blocking the render thread, working across all supported GPU backends.
A new NuGet package wraps the Silk.NET Vulkan interop layer, making it straightforward to wire up Vulkan contexts without custom P/Invoke boilerplate.
All .sln solution files are converted to the new .slnx format, improving IDE compatibility and reducing merge conflicts.

bullets.lead: Binding generation is now deterministic across platforms
bullets.detail: The binding generator now produces identical output regardless of the host OS, eliminating spurious diffs when regenerating on different machines.
The SpanIterator held a raw pointer into the parent SKRegion. If the parent was collected first the pointer dangled. The region is now kept alive for the iterator's lifetime.

bullets.lead: Native use-after-free in SKPixmap.ExtractSubset and With* fixed
bullets.detail: SKPixmap methods that return a derived pixmap were not rooting the pixel-source object, allowing it to be collected while the derived pixmap was still in use.

bullets.lead: CoTaskMem pixel-buffer leak in SKImage.Create raster failure path fixed
bullets.detail: A native pixel buffer allocated during raster image creation was not freed when the native call failed, causing a silent native memory leak.

The per-type reflection check that decides whether to skip handle registration was repeated on every object construction. It is now cached per type, eliminating repeated reflection overhead in object-creation hot paths.
SKData.SaveTo previously copied data into an intermediate buffer before writing. The copy is now avoided, halving memory usage on this path.
The null-terminated fast path in GetEncodedText no longer allocates an intermediate string.
The uniform lookup map is now pre-sized to the known uniform count, eliminating resizing overhead.

bullets.lead: FreeType font rendering on Windows Nano Server
bullets.detail: Nano Server environments lack the GDI font stack. SkiaSharp now falls back to FreeType on Nano Server, enabling text rendering in containerised Windows workloads that was previously broken.

bullets.lead: Azure Linux, Alpine/musl, and Nano Server test targets added
bullets.detail: Containerised CI test legs for Azure Linux, Alpine (musl libc), and Nano Server validate SkiaSharp on production-relevant Linux environments.

bullets.lead: Windows MSVC environment initialized once per native build
bullets.detail: The MSVC toolchain environment is now set up once per build rather than once per compilation unit, significantly reducing native build times on Windows.

contributor_summaries.jeffska: Implemented FreeType font support for Windows Nano Server, unblocking text rendering in GDI-less container environments.
contributor_summaries.mmitche: Fixed native build performance on Windows by initializing the MSVC environment once per build instead of per compilation unit.
contributor_summaries.ramezgerges: Authored the Graphite GPU backend bindings for Vulkan, Metal, and Dawn.
